cards.t: Increase by r% → multiply by (1 + r/100). Decrease by r% → multiply by (1 − r/100). Successive changes multiply: +20% then −20% gives 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, a 4% fall, not zero.
Profit% = (SP − CP)/CP × 100. Always measure against CP unless told otherwise. Marked price (MP) → discount on MP → selling price. SP = MP × (1 − d/100).
The base matters: 'A is 25% more than B' means B is 20% less than A. Two successive discounts of a% and b% equal a + b − ab/100 overall, never a + b.
SI = P·r·t/100. Amount = P + SI. Interest grows in a straight line because it is always on the original principal.
A = P(1 + r/100)ⁿ. For half-yearly compounding use rate r/2 and 2n periods; quarterly: r/4 and 4n. CI = A − P.
For 2 years, CI − SI = P(r/100)². Money doubles in about 72/r years (rule of 72). Different rates in different years: multiply the factors one after another.
a : b = c : d means ad = bc. To combine A:B = 2:3 and B:C = 4:5, make B equal: A:B:C = 8:12:15. Work in 'units' and find the value of one unit last.
Profit is shared in proportion to (capital × time). If capitals are invested for different periods, multiply each capital by its months before taking the ratio.
Direct proportion: y/x constant. Inverse proportion: xy constant. If a:b = 3:4 and total is 140, the parts are 60 and 80 (140 ÷ 7 = 20 per unit).
Average = total ÷ count. Work with totals: if the average of 5 numbers is 20, the total is 100. Adding a number x changes the total by x.
Average = Σ(weight × value)/Σ(weight). When two groups with averages a and b are mixed, the overall average lies between them, closer to the larger group.
If every item is increased by k, the average rises by k. If a new item replaces an old one, the average changes by (new − old)/count.
When two items with values a < b are mixed to get a mean m, the quantity ratio (cheaper : dearer) = (b − m) : (m − a).
A container holds V litres of pure liquid. Remove x litres and replace with water, n times. Pure left = V(1 − x/V)ⁿ.
Draw the cross diagram: put the mean in the middle, the two values at the corners, and subtract diagonally. The differences give the ratio.
D = S × T. km/h → m/s: multiply by 5/18. Average speed over equal distances is the harmonic mean 2ab/(a + b), not (a + b)/2.
Same direction: subtract speeds. Opposite directions: add speeds. A train of length L crossing a pole takes L/S; crossing a platform of length P takes (L + P)/S.
Downstream speed = b + s; upstream = b − s. So b = (down + up)/2 and s = (down − up)/2. For races, work out who covers how much in the same time.
If A finishes in a days, A's rate is 1/a of the work per day. Together: 1/a + 1/b per day, so time = ab/(a + b).
Assume total work = LCM of the times; each person's daily output becomes an integer. Inlet pipes add, outlet pipes subtract.
Money is divided in the ratio of work done (rate × days), not just days worked.

HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers. Use prime factorisation: HCF takes the lowest powers, LCM the highest. For 'greatest number dividing a, b, c leaving remainders', take the HCF of the differences.
3 and 9: digit sum. 4: last two digits. 8: last three digits. 11: difference between sums of alternate digits. 7, 11, 13: use the 1001 trick on groups of three digits.
If N = pᵃ qᵇ rᶜ, the number of factors is (a + 1)(b + 1)(c + 1). The sum of the factors is the product of (1 + p + … + pᵃ) for each prime.
Digits 2, 3, 7, 8 repeat every 4 powers; 4 and 9 every 2; 0, 1, 5, 6 never change. Divide the exponent by the cycle length and use the remainder (0 means the last place in the cycle).
Remainders can be multiplied and added: (a·b) mod n = ((a mod n)(b mod n)) mod n. Useful: aⁿ + bⁿ is divisible by a + b for odd n; aⁿ − bⁿ by a − b always.
The power of a prime p in n! = ⌊n/p⌋ + ⌊n/p²⌋ + …. Trailing zeros in n! are the power of 5. Wilson: (p − 1)! ≡ −1 (mod p) for prime p.
ax² + bx + c = 0 has roots (−b ± √D)/2a with D = b² − 4ac. Sum = −b/a, product = c/a. D > 0: two real roots; D = 0: equal roots; D < 0: no real roots.
Never solve for the roots if you can avoid it: α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ; 1/α + 1/β = (α + β)/αβ; (α − β)² = (α + β)² − 4αβ.
Remainder theorem: the remainder of p(x) ÷ (x − a) is p(a). Factor theorem: (x − a) is a factor if p(a) = 0. A cubic with roots α, β, γ has sum = −b/a and product = −d/a.
nth term aₙ = a + (n − 1)d; sum Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d]. Three terms in AP: a − d, a, a + d.
aₙ = arⁿ⁻¹; sum Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1); infinite sum a/(1 − r) when |r| < 1. Geometric mean of two numbers is √(ab).
Σn = n(n + 1)/2, Σn² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6, Σn³ = (n(n + 1)/2)². For telescoping series like 1/(k(k + 1)), write it as 1/k − 1/(k + 1).

Algebra: Coordinate Geometry.blurb: Lines and circles on a plane.

cards.t: Slope m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). Line: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁). Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular lines have m₁m₂ = −1. Distance from (p, q) to ax + by + c = 0 is |ap + bq + c|/√(a² + b²).
The point dividing (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) in ratio m : n internally is ((mx₂ + nx₁)/(m + n), (my₂ + ny₁)/(m + n)). The midpoint uses m = n.
(x − h)² + (y − k)² = r². The tangent at a point is perpendicular to the radius. Area of a triangle with vertices (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂), (x₃, y₃) is ½|x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|.

Algebra: Sets & Relations.blurb: Collections and the rules that link them.

cards.t: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B). A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets. A − B means in A but not in B.
A relation from A to B is a subset of A × B. Reflexive: (a, a) always present. Symmetric: (a, b) implies (b, a). Transitive: (a, b) and (b, c) imply (a, c). Equivalence = all three.
If |A| = m and |B| = n, there are 2^(mn) relations from A to B. Check each property by testing a few pairs, then look for a counter-example.

Algebra: Functions.blurb: Rules that turn inputs into outputs.

cards.t: Domain: allowed inputs (avoid division by zero, even roots of negatives, logs of non-positives). Range: the outputs actually produced.
One-one: different inputs give different outputs. Onto: every element of the codomain is hit. A function from a set with m elements to one with n elements: nᵐ functions; one-one (m ≤ n): n!/(n − m)!.
(f∘g)(x) = f(g(x)). The inverse swaps x and y and exists only for one-one, onto functions. Functional equations: plug in smart values such as 0, 1 or −x.

Algebra: Modulus & Logarithms.blurb: Absolute values and exponents in reverse.

cards.t: |x| = x if x ≥ 0, −x if x < 0. |x| < a ⇔ −a < x < a. |x| > a ⇔ x > a or x < −a. |x − a| is the distance of x from a.
log(ab) = log a + log b; log(a/b) = log a − log b; log aⁿ = n log a; log_b a = log a / log b. Arguments must be positive; check every solution at the end.
Convert logs to exponents: log_b x = y ⇔ x = bʸ. For inequalities with base < 1, the inequality flips. For modulus equations, split into cases at the point where the inside is zero.
Angle sum 180°. Exterior angle = sum of the two opposite interior angles. Similar triangles have sides in equal ratio and areas in the square of that ratio. Pythagoras: a² + b² = c².
Area = ½ × base × height = ½ab sin C = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)) with s the semi-perimeter. Equilateral: (√3/4)a². The medians meet at the centroid, which divides each in the ratio 2 : 1.
Interior angle sum = (n − 2) × 180°. Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 360°/n. Number of diagonals = n(n − 3)/2.
Angle at the centre = 2 × angle at the circumference on the same arc. Angles in the same segment are equal. Tangents from an external point are equal. Chord length = 2√(r² − d²).
Circle: πr², 2πr. Sector: (θ/360)πr². Cylinder: V = πr²h, curved area 2πrh. Cone: V = ⅓πr²h, slant l = √(r² + h²), curved area πrl. Sphere: V = 4/3 πr³, area 4πr².
When a solid is melted and recast, volume is conserved. Equate the volumes and solve for the unknown dimension.
sin = opposite/hypotenuse, cos = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan = opposite/adjacent. sin²θ + cos²θ = 1; 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ. Learn sin/cos/tan of 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°.
sin(A ± B) = sinA cosB ± cosA sinB; cos(A ± B) = cosA cosB ∓ sinA sinB; sin2A = 2 sinA cosA; cos2A = cos²A − sin²A.
Draw the right triangle, mark the angle of elevation or depression, then pick the ratio that links the known and unknown sides.
n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = Σn(X) − Σn(X ∩ Y) + n(A ∩ B ∩ C). Fill a Venn diagram from the centre outwards.
Exactly one = Σn(X) − 2·Σ pairwise + 3·all three. Exactly two = Σ pairwise − 3·all three. At least two = exactly two + all three.
Minimum overlap of groups of sizes a and b in a population N is max(0, a + b − N); maximum overlap is min(a, b).
Multiplication rule for 'and', addition for 'or'. nPr = n!/(n − r)!; nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!). Arrangements with repeats: n!/(p!q!…). Circular arrangements: (n − 1)!.
Gap method for 'no two together': arrange the others first and insert into gaps. For 'together', glue into a block. For 'at least one', subtract the none-case from the total.

Identical objects into distinct boxes (non-negative): C(n + k − 1, k − 1). Each box at least one: C(n − 1, k − 1). If every box needs a minimum, give each box its minimum first and distribute what is left.
P(E) = favourable/total outcomes. P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). Independent events: P(A and B) = P(A)P(B). Complement: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none).
P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). Count only inside the reduced sample space B. Bayes: P(A | B) = P(B | A)P(A)/P(B).

Variance = mean of squares − square of mean. Adding k to every value shifts the mean but not the spread; multiplying by a scales the mean by a, the SD by |a| and the variance by a². Expected value = Σ value × probability.
Check units, the base for every percentage and the time period. Percentage change = (new − old)/old × 100. Percentage points differ from percentage change.
Approximate early and round only at the end. Convert percentages to fractions you know (12.5% = 1/8, 16.67% = 1/6). Compare ratios by cross-multiplying rather than dividing.
1 hectare = 10,000 m²; 1 m³ = 1000 L; km/h → m/s ×5/18. Always check whether a table gives values or percentages.
Read the scale and gridlines, then list the values you need. For growth, always use the earlier year as the base. A steeper line is a bigger change in absolute terms, not necessarily in percentage.
Percentages sum to 100 and angles to 360 (1% = 3.6°). The slice of a different pie cannot be compared unless the totals are known.
If one chart shows revenue and another shows a margin or share, multiply them. Highest percentage does not mean highest absolute value.
A + B adds entries. AB needs columns of A = rows of B, and AB ≠ BA in general. (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ. A is symmetric if Aᵀ = A; skew-symmetric if Aᵀ = −A.
2×2: ad − bc. For 3×3, expand along any row. |AB| = |A||B|; |kA| = kⁿ|A| for an n×n matrix; |Aᵀ| = |A|. A matrix is singular when its determinant is 0.
Minor Mᵢⱼ: determinant after deleting row i and column j. Cofactor Cᵢⱼ = (−1)ⁱ⁺ʲ Mᵢⱼ. Expanding using another row's cofactors gives 0.
adj A is the transpose of the cofactor matrix. A·adj A = |A|·I; A⁻¹ = adj A/|A|. |adj A| = |A|ⁿ⁻¹; |A⁻¹| = 1/|A|.
For AX = B with |A| ≠ 0: unique solution X = A⁻¹B (Cramer: xᵢ = Dᵢ/D). If |A| = 0: either infinitely many solutions or none, depending on consistency.
Area of a triangle = ½|det [x y 1]|. Three points are collinear if that determinant is 0. Matrix powers: look for patterns such as A² = A, A² = I or nilpotent forms.
Try substitution first. For 0/0 factor and cancel, rationalise, or use standard limits: sin x/x → 1, (eˣ − 1)/x → 1, ln(1 + x)/x → 1, (1 − cos x)/x² → ½. At infinity, divide by the highest power.
f is continuous at a if the left limit, right limit and f(a) are all equal. To find an unknown constant, equate them.
Differentiable implies continuous, not the other way round. |x| has a corner at 0, so it is not differentiable there. Check the left and right derivatives separately.
Power: (xⁿ)′ = nxⁿ⁻¹. Product: (uv)′ = u′v + uv′. Quotient: (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v². Chain: d/dx f(g(x)) = f′(g(x))g′(x). (eᵃˣ)′ = aeᵃˣ; (ln x)′ = 1/x.
Tangent slope = f′(a). Increasing where f′ > 0. Maxima/minima: f′ = 0, then check the sign change or f″ (negative → maximum). Optimisation: express in one variable, differentiate, set to zero.
Link the variables in one equation, differentiate both sides with respect to time, then substitute the known values.
∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C (n ≠ −1); ∫1/x dx = ln|x| + C; ∫eˣ dx = eˣ + C; ∫sin x = −cos x; ∫cos x = sin x; ∫sec²x = tan x. Always add C.
Choose u as the inner function whose derivative appears elsewhere. ∫f(ax + b) dx = F(ax + b)/a + C.
∫u dv = uv − ∫v du; choose u by LIATE (Log, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential). Split rational functions into partial fractions before integrating.
∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a). If you substitute, change the limits too.
∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = ∫ₐᵇ f(a + b − x)dx. Even function over [−a, a]: 2∫₀ᵃ. Odd function: 0. Over a periodic function's n periods: n × (one period).
Area between y = f(x) and the x-axis from a to b is ∫|f| dx. Between two curves: ∫(top − bottom) dx between their intersection points.
Draw the Venn diagram for the most flexible arrangement of the statements, then try to break each conclusion. A conclusion follows only if it holds in every valid diagram.

All A are B: A inside B. No A is B: separate circles. Some A are B: overlap. Some A are not B: part of A outside B. 'Some' always includes the possibility of 'all', but 'some are not' does not guarantee it.
Ignore real-world facts. 'All A are B' does not mean 'All B are A'. Two negatives give no conclusion. Look for complementary pairs (some … / some … not) only when the question says 'either–or'.

LR: Linear & Circular Seating.blurb: Build the arrangement step by step.

cards.t: Write the positions 1…n. Place fixed positions first, then 'immediate' clues, then relative clues. In 'facing north' rows, left is the reader's left.
A person's left is the next seat clockwise; right is anticlockwise. 'Second to the left of A' means two seats clockwise. In a table of n people, the opposite seat is n/2 away.
Fix one person first in a circle. Keep both possibilities open when a clue allows two; the next clue usually decides.
Draw a row of days or slots. Immediate-before clues create blocks; gap clues fix distances. Start with exact-day clues.
List where each person can and cannot be. Use elimination: if a person has one remaining slot, fix it and update the rest.
Test the final schedule against every clue before choosing an answer.
Combine 'A is taller than B' and 'B is taller than C' into A > B > C. Rank from the top plus rank from the bottom equals total + 1.
Number of people between positions p and q is |p − q| − 1.
If two chains cannot be joined, the question is usually asking about something that can still be determined; don't force a full order.
Use squares for males and circles for females, = for marriage, vertical lines for children. Fix gender whenever the text gives it.

Father's sister = paternal aunt; mother's brother = maternal uncle; sibling's child = nephew/niece; spouse's sibling = brother/sister-in-law. 'Mother's only son' = brother (if the speaker has no other brother) or the speaker.
Decode each symbol to a relation, then apply them in order from the first person onwards. Keep track of the gender of each person in the chain.
A right turn rotates your heading clockwise: N → E → S → W. A left turn goes anticlockwise. Track east–west and north–south displacement separately.
Straight-line distance = √(net east² + net north²). Direction of the end point from the start is determined by the signs of the net displacements.
In the morning the sun is in the east, so shadows fall west. In the evening they fall east.
Compare each pair of letters: a constant shift, alternating shifts, mirror letters (A↔Z), reversal or swapped positions. Test the rule on every letter, not just the first.
Find a word common to two phrases; the code common to both is its code. Eliminate known pairs to decode the rest.
Letter values A = 1 … Z = 26 are the usual base. Watch for position weights and vowel-only rules.
Check differences, then differences of differences, then ratios. Try squares, cubes (±k), primes, alternating series and 'term × k + c'.
Convert to numbers (A = 1). Separate interleaved series. For letter–number clusters, treat letters and numbers as two series.
Find the pattern from the majority; the term that breaks it is the odd one.
A = 1, B = 2 … Z = 26; the mirror of a letter at position p is 27 − p. Learn EJOTY (5, 10, 15, 20, 25) as anchors.
Write the forward/backward gap between consecutive letters in each group. Three share the same pattern; one doesn't.
For triads like FROM–RMFO–OFMR, find where each letter moves in the first step and then in the second; apply both to the new word.
In 29 → 841 → 752 → 784, the first step is squaring, then subtract 89, then add 32. Verify with the second example before trusting the rule.
Squares, cubes, ×k, ±k, digit sums and reversals. Check that the same constants appear in every example.
Apply the rule to each option's first number and compare the second and third numbers.
Answer the question with Statement I alone, then II alone, then both together. 'Sufficient' means exactly one possible answer.
I alone, II alone, either alone, both together but neither alone, or not even together. Do not use outside knowledge.
Draw every arrangement that fits a statement. If different arrangements give different answers, the statement is not sufficient.
A valid course addresses the problem named in the statement, directly and proportionately. Reject extreme, irrelevant or harmful steps.
A reason explains the statement only if it plausibly brings about the stated outcome. Facts about the same place that have nothing to do with the outcome are not reasons.
An implicit assumption is something the statement takes for granted. Options with absolute words ('all', 'never', 'only') are rarely assumed.
Read the whole sentence first and guess the meaning before looking at the options. Decide if the word is positive or negative.
Break unknown words into prefix, root and suffix: benevolent = bene (good) + vol (wish).
The opposite word often appears among the options. Choose by meaning, not by similar sound.
Define the word in your own words, flip it, then match. Check that the part of speech matches.
un-, in-, im-, dis- and mal- often negate meaning, but not always (e.g. 'inflammable').
The synonym is nearly always an option. Re-read the question for the word 'opposite'.
Decide whether the blank needs a positive, negative or neutral word, and what part of speech.
Look for contrast words (but, although) and cause words (because, hence) to decide direction.
Substitute the final choice into the sentence and read it aloud.
Learn words in families and in sentences, not as isolated lists. Revisit words after 1, 3, 7 and 21 days.
Use roots such as bene (good), mal (bad), chron (time), anthrop (human), loqu (speak) to decode new words.
Cross out options that are clearly wrong in tone before choosing between the last two.
Idioms rarely mean what the words say. Guess from the situation the idiom is used in.
Remember each idiom with one short example sentence.
Literal options are almost always wrong.
-cide (killing), -phobia (fear), -cracy (rule), -ology (study), omni- (all), poly- (many).
Omniscient (knows all) vs omnipotent (all-powerful) vs omnipresent (everywhere); emigrate (leave) vs immigrate (arrive).
Match the root, then check the full phrase.
Say it in a sentence: 'A is used for B', 'A is part of B', 'A is the opposite of B'.
Test the same sentence on each option pair.
Keep the order of the pair; reversing it changes the relationship.
Ignore phrases between subject and verb: 'The list of items IS'. 'Along with', 'together with', 'as well as' do not change the number.
Each, every, either, neither, one of → singular. A number of → plural; the number of → singular. Neither … nor: nearest subject decides.
Collective nouns take singular when acting as a unit and plural when members act individually. Plural-only nouns: scissors, police, cattle.
interested in, good at, depend on, capable of, prefer X to Y, different from, responsible for.
'Discuss about' and 'despite of' are wrong. 'Since' goes with a point in time, 'for' with a period.
If the pair feels natural when said aloud, trust it; otherwise check the list.
Present perfect: from past to now (since, for). Past perfect: earlier of two past events. Do not use present perfect with a finished time such as 'yesterday'.
If + present → will; if + past → would; if + past perfect → would have + past participle.
Enjoy, avoid, finish + -ing; decide, hope, want + to-infinitive; look forward to + -ing.
Use 'an' before a vowel sound (an hour), 'a' before a consonant sound (a university). 'The' for specific or unique things, rivers, oceans and superlatives.
Use the subject form after 'than' only if a verb can follow ('taller than I (am)'). After prepositions use the object form: between you and me.
Little/much with uncountable nouns; few/many with countable nouns. 'A few' is positive; 'few' is negative.
Subject–verb agreement, tense, preposition, article, pronoun agreement, parallel structure, word choice.
Read each part slowly and ask what rule it could break. The error is usually one word, so look at verbs and prepositions first.
If every rule passes, 'no error' may be the answer — but try each part twice first.
affect (verb) / effect (noun); lose / loose; accept / except; principal / principle; stationary / stationery; complement / compliment.
Principal is your pal (a person); stationery has an 'e' like envelope; lose has one 'o' fewer than loose.
Decide the part of speech needed in the blank, then the meaning.
The first sentence introduces the topic without pointers like 'this', 'however' or 'they'.
Link sentences by pronouns, connectors (therefore, however) and repeated nouns. Mini-pairs often appear in the options.
The last sentence usually concludes or gives a consequence.
Find the main topic from the majority; the odd one shifts topic, even if it uses similar words.
An opening sentence works alone. A closing sentence sums up or looks ahead.
Read the paragraph without the suspect sentence to see whether it flows.
Note the main idea of each paragraph in a few words. Identify the author's tone from the adjectives used.
Main idea, detail, inference, tone, vocabulary-in-context and application. Detail questions are answered directly in the passage; inference questions need a small step beyond it.
Wrong options are often too extreme, out of scope or reversed. Prefer the option that paraphrases the passage.
